query: Are there particular sectors I should reduce as I approach retirement, and which ones should I keep for income generation?

recommendations.title: Reduce Technology and Energy Exposure for Retirement Glide Path
recommendations.summary: Decrease allocation to higher-volatility Technology (18%) and cyclical Energy (8%) sectors to align with approaching retirement and moderate risk tolerance.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: At 55 with a 10-year retirement timeline, you should begin reducing exposure to volatile growth sectors. Technology, while representing 18% of your portfolio, carries higher volatility and is sensitive to interest rate changes. Energy (8%) is highly cyclical and volatile, making it less suitable for capital preservation as you near retirement. Recommend reducing Technology from 18% to 10-12% and Energy from 8% to 3-5% over the next 2-3 years. Reallocate proceeds to income-generating sectors and bonds to smooth your glide path while maintaining some growth potential.
recommendations.suggested_action: Gradually reduce Technology and Energy sector weightings

recommendations.title: Maintain and Potentially Increase Healthcare and Consumer Staples for Income
recommendations.summary: Keep strong Healthcare (22%) and Consumer Staples (10%) allocations as defensive, dividend-paying sectors ideal for retirement income generation.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: Healthcare (22%) and Consumer Staples (10%) are excellent retirement sectors offering defensive characteristics, consistent dividends, and recession resistance. Your holdings JNJ, UNH, and PG are high-quality dividend aristocrats with 40+ year histories of dividend growth. Healthcare demand remains stable regardless of economic cycles, and these companies typically yield 2-3% with annual dividend growth of 5-8%. Consumer Staples provide similar defensive qualities. These sectors should form the core of your equity allocation (combined 35-40%) as you transition to retirement, providing reliable income while maintaining purchasing power through dividend growth.
recommendations.suggested_action: Hold current positions; consider increasing Consumer Staples to 12-15%

recommendations.title: Add Utilities and REITs for Enhanced Retirement Income
recommendations.summary: Introduce Utilities (4-6%) and REITs (3-5%) to diversify income sources and achieve 3.5-4.5% portfolio yield for retirement needs.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: Your current portfolio lacks dedicated income-generating sectors beyond Healthcare and Consumer Staples. To support your retirement income goal of $80-100k annually (4.4-5.6% of projected portfolio), you need higher-yielding, stable sectors. Utilities typically yield 3-4% with regulated, predictable cash flows and low correlation to economic cycles. REITs offer 3-5% yields with inflation protection through rent escalations. Adding 8-10% combined allocation to these sectors would increase your overall portfolio yield from approximately 2.2% to 3.0-3.5%, providing $25,500-$29,750 in annual dividend income (on $850k). Consider VPU (Utilities ETF) and VNQ (REIT ETF) for diversified exposure.

recommendations.title: Maintain Financials Allocation with Quality Focus
recommendations.summary: Retain Financials (18%) position with JPM and BRK.B as they offer income, value characteristics, and benefit from stable interest rate environment.
recommendations.detailed_rationale: Your 18% Financials allocation through quality holdings JPM and BRK.B is appropriate for your retirement glide path. Financials benefit from a stabilizing interest rate environment and these specific holdings offer defensive characteristics: JPM yields ~2.5% with strong capital return programs and fortress balance sheet, while BRK.B provides diversified exposure, capital appreciation potential, and Buffett's defensive positioning. Financials are less volatile than Technology while offering better growth potential than pure bond alternatives. This 18% allocation strikes an appropriate balance - large enough to contribute meaningfully to returns but not overweight. Hold current positions; avoid increasing beyond 20% to maintain diversification.
